html:
From 1658 to 1834 the Cape Colony ran on the labour of enslaved people. The Dutch East India Company (VOC) brought the first shiploads in 1658, six years after the Dutch settled the Cape.

Unlike most colonies, the Cape drew its slaves from all around the Indian Ocean: from West Africa, Madagascar and Mozambique, and through the Dutch slave trade in Asia from India, Ceylon and Indonesia. For much of the 1700s there were more slaves than free settlers. They worked farms, vineyards and households in Cape Town.

Their descendants include the Cape Malay and Coloured communities. They helped shape the Afrikaans language, and brought Islam to the Cape. Britain took the colony in 1806, banned the slave trade in 1807, and freed the slaves under the Slavery Abolition Act in 1834, though they had to keep working for their owners as "apprentices" until 1838.
